questions.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ -6 & -7\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}a & -1 \\ b & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $D={P}^{-1}AP,$ find the value of  $\frac{b}{a}.$
questions.worked_solution:
From the diagonal matrix $D=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]$, we deduce that the eigenvalues of $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-1.$

So, the  first column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-4.$ 

Now, we simply need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{1}=-4.$ Computing $A-(-4)I,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-4)I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ -6 & -7\end{aligned}]-(-4)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6 & 3 \\ -6 & -3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}6 & 3 & 0 \\ -6 & -3 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{1}+{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}6 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

 

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=2,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $\frac{b}{a}=\frac{2}{-1}=-2.$

questions.problem:
Determine if the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}6 & 5 \\ -10 & -9\end{aligned}]$ 
is diagonalizable or not, and if it is diagonalizable, find a corresponding diagonal matrix $D.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ by solving $det(A-\lambda I)=0$:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}6-\lambda  & 5 \\ -10 & -9-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (6-\lambda )(-9-\lambda )-(5)(-10) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+3\lambda -4 & =0 \\ (\lambda -1)(\lambda +4) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-4.$ Since we get two distinct eigenvalues, the matrix $A$ is diagonalizable.

Now, we construct the diagonal matrix $D,$ as follows:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}]
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the matrix $K$ for which ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-5$ are eigenvalues, and

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]
$$

are the respective eigenvectors. What are the values of $a,b,c$ given that

$$
K=[\begin{aligned}b & 1 \\ 0 & c\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & a\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}b & 1 \\ 0 & c\end{aligned}]}^{-1}?
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-5,$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -5\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=2,$ and

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=-5.$

Therefore, we get

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
K=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -5\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}.
$$

 

In conclusion, we get  $a=-5,$ $b=-1,$ and $c=-1.$

questions.problem:
Consider the matrix $B$ for which ${\lambda }_{1}=5$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-3$ are eigenvalues, and

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 4\end{aligned}]
$$

are the respective eigenvectors. What are the values of $a,b,c$ given that

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}b & -3 \\ c & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}a & 0 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}b & -3 \\ c & 4\end{aligned}]}^{-1}?
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=5$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-3,$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=5,$ and

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=-3.$

Therefore, we get

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ -1 & 4\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ -1 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ -1 & 4\end{aligned}]}^{-1}.
$$

 

In conclusion, we get  $a=5,$ $b=1,$ and $c=-1.$

questions.problem:
Determine if the matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]$
is diagonalizable or not, and if it is diagonalizable, find a corresponding diagonal matrix $D.$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $A$ is triangular, the eigenvalues are the entries on the main diagonal. 

So, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=-2.$ Since we get one repeated eigenvalue, the matrix might not be diagonalizable. To check this, we row-reduce the matrix $(A-(-2)I)\text{x}=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]+2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 3 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has only $1$ pivot column. This implies that we will have only $2-1=1$ linearly independent eigenvector corresponding to the current eigenvalue. Therefore, $A$ is not diagonalizable.
